name: The Right to an Explanation
title: The Right to an Explanation
answer: The right to an explanation is a legal claim that a person can ask for the logic behind an automated decision that affects them. It sits in data protection, consumer, employment, and administrative law, and it overlaps with the duty to give reasons in public law. In practice it covers decisions such as credit refusals, hiring screens, benefit calculations, and content moderation, though the exact trigger varies by jurisdiction. The right is not one single rule, it is a family of rights to information, access, and contestation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: The right to an explanation is a legal claim that a person can ask for the logic behind an automated decision that affects them. It sits in data protection, consumer, employment, and administrative law, and it overlaps with the duty to give reasons in public law. In practice it covers decisions such as credit refusals, hiring screens, benefit calculations, and content moderation, though the exact trigger varies by jurisdiction. The right is not one single rule, it is a family of rights to information, access, and contestation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The right runs on the records and systems that produced the decision. That includes the model, its training data, feature definitions, version history, logs, and the human review steps around it. It also runs on the organisation's ability to retrieve those records after the fact, because an explanation is only as good as the audit trail behind it. In many cases the practical limit is not the law but whether the data pipeline kept the necessary evidence.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Lawyers and compliance teams map the decision path, identify the legal basis, and match the request to the relevant statutory right. Technical teams then produce model documentation, feature importance, counterfactual examples, or plain language summaries, depending on the standard. The work often involves a joint exercise between legal, data, and product staff, with a written response that separates the decision rule from the individual's case. Some explanations are generated automatically, others are drafted by hand for high stakes decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The right to an explanation creates duties to preserve provenance, meaning who built the model, what data trained it, and what changes were made. It also creates risk if explanations are incomplete, misleading, or inconsistent with the actual system, which can lead to regulatory action or litigation. On this site, the topic sits within 219 compliance and regulation pages and 29 AI case law precedents, showing how quickly the area is being tested. The main tension is between trade secrets and the individual's need for a meaningful reason.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more specific and more operational duties, with regulators asking for explanations that are understandable to the person affected. We can expect standardised formats, model cards, and decision logs to become part of ordinary compliance. The 6948 state AI bills tracked on this site suggest that many legislatures are trying to define explanation rights in their own terms. Over time the right may shift from a general data protection principle to a concrete set of documentation and response requirements.
